gh issue create --title "Below fourteen rows there is no conversation and no prompt, only panels" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Problem

Shrink a full-screen game to 13 rows or fewer and the panels become the
entire screen. The message window is gone, so the player sees no
conversation, no `COMMAND>` prompt, and no sign the game is waiting for
them. It is: typing a command still works, blind.

The threshold is **fourteen** rows. At 72x14 the prompt is on the last
line and the game reads normally; at 72x13 it is not on screen at all.

## Why

`make_windows()` (`tui.c`) places the message window at row `PANELH`
with `msgh = LINES-PANELH > 1 ? LINES-PANELH : 1`. Once `LINES <=
PANELH` that row is off the bottom of the screen, so the window exists
but nothing of it is visible. The clamp to 1 keeps it from being zero
rows tall; it does not keep it on screen.

## Scope

Pre-existing, and reachable only by resizing mid-game — startup still
refuses below 72x24 and prints `Terminal too small (need 72x24) --
using classic display.`

Distinct from the two neighbours:

- #88 is about the display not coming *back* after a shrink. This is
  what is on screen while you are down there.
- #91 was the panel rows colliding, now fixed. That fix makes this one
  more visible rather than less: the panels are now well-formed at
  every height, so a player at 12 rows sees a tidy display that simply
  never responds.

## Suggested approach

Worth deciding rather than patching, and it is the same question #78
raised and answered for width:

- Give the message window the rows the panels cannot use — draw fewer
  panel rows once the terminal is short, so the conversation always has
  a line or two. The panels already clip from the bottom after #91, so
  the mechanism exists.
- Or accept panels-only and say so on screen, which needs a line the
  panels do not have.

The first keeps the player able to play. The second is cheaper and
worse.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] At any height the game accepts commands at, the prompt is
      visible.
- [ ] Covered in `tests/tui.sh`, which now sweeps heights.
- [ ] `README.md`'s sentence about there being no room for the
      conversation goes with the fix.

build of that branch's merge-base. Follow the workflow in

fix(tui): clip the panels by row as well as by column

#78 bounded the panel draw loops by column. Nothing bounded them by
row, and tui_refresh_panels() asks for all eleven lines however short
the terminal is. Two ways to fail, one on each side of the last row: at
twelve rows the tenth grid line was drawn onto the bottom border, and
at eleven wmove() failed outright, left the cursor where the previous
line had left it, and the whole line landed on the row above --
`mq 9  . . . . . . . . . .10 .x`, two grid rows and a border sharing
one line.

panel_has_row() asks what panel_room() asks on the other axis, and both
draw loops return early when the row is not inside the box. That alone
fixed the quadrant panel and not the status panel, which turned out to
be a second defect: make_windows() resized the status panel back to its
full PANELH rows on every repaint whatever the screen height, so it
stayed taller than the screen, its bottom border fell off the bottom,
and its last line was drawn where that border should have been. It now
takes the height the screen can show, as the quadrant panel already did
by way of resize_term().

A third, found by ui-review: the SENSORS DAMAGED caption still named
row PANELH-1 absolutely, so from twelve rows down the dashes lost their
explanation entirely -- the field of nothing with no reason given that
the caption exists to prevent, at the sizes where a player is least
sure what they are looking at. It now asks the window where its bottom
border is.

Rows clip in silence, unlike the columns #78 marked with `>`. A

content.text:
Two things about `/codex:adversarial-review` change what the workflow can say, so let me settle them before editing AGENTS.md.

**It cannot be invoked by an agent.** Its frontmatter sets `disable-model-invocation: true` — which is why it's absent from my skills list while `codex:rescue` and `codex:setup` appear. Only a human typing `/codex:adversarial-review` can start it. The underlying runtime (`codex-companion.mjs`) is reachable from Bash, but going that way deliberately bypasses the gate the plugin author put there, including its own wait-vs-background prompt.

The rest checks out: `codex-cli 0.147.0` is on PATH, the review is explicitly review-only ("Do not fix issues, apply patches"), it takes focus text, and it returns a structured `approve` / `needs-attention` verdict with severity-ranked findings — which fits step 8's gate cleanly.

questions.question: The agent can't invoke /codex:adversarial-review — the plugin blocks model invocation. How should the workflow get that review?

options.label: You run it at the gate (Recommended)
options.description: AGENTS.md step 8 says the agent stops before committing, reports what it changed, and asks you to run /codex:adversarial-review. It then addresses every finding and re-runs the pass. Faithful to the plugin's design and to how the command bills; costs the agent's ability to finish a slice unattended.

options.label: Agent shells out to the runtime
options.description: The agent runs `node <plugin>/scripts/codex-companion.mjs adversarial-review ...` directly from Bash, discovering the plugin path. Keeps unattended runs working, but bypasses the author's disable-model-invocation decision and the wait/background prompt, and the versioned path breaks on plugin upgrade.

options.label: You run it, agent falls back
options.description: Prefer your /codex:adversarial-review when you're present; if the agent is running unattended it uses the existing code-review sub-agent instead and says so in the commit. Two review paths to keep in step, which is the failure mode AGENTS.md's 'Point at the definitions here' rule exists to prevent.

questions.question: Should Codex replace the existing code-review sub-agent, or run alongside it?

options.label: Alongside — Codex challenges, sub-agent gates (Recommended)
options.description: Codex attacks the design and approach; .claude/agents/code-review.md stays the step 8 gate. Keeps what Codex's prompt explicitly excludes: the ui-review disclosure enforcement, the golden-recording rule, C/CMake specifics, and the 'review coverage' mandate. Costs a second pass per commit.

options.label: Replace — Codex is the code reviewer
options.description: What you asked for literally. /codex:adversarial-review becomes the step 8 gate and .claude/agents/code-review.md is retired. Note what goes with it: Codex's prompt says to report only material runtime findings and to skip style, naming and cleanup, so the repo-specific mandates would have to move into the focus text passed on every invocation — and nothing enforces that they were.

options.label: Replace, and port the mandates
options.description: Codex becomes the gate, and I write the repo-specific mandates into a checked-in focus file that AGENTS.md tells you to pass as focus text every time, so they survive the swap rather than depending on memory.

### The review sub-agents

Steps 6-8 invoke Claude Code sub-agents defined in `.claude/agents/`:
`ui-review`, `verifier` and `code-review`. What matters is not the tool. It
is that the work is judged by a reader who did not write it, and who
reaches its conclusions from the diff rather than from a memory of having
intended something.

Which of the three bind depends on what changed. `code-review` binds on
every commit, without exception — it is the gate step 8 describes.
`verifier` binds as well, with the scope step 7 already gives it: the
checks appropriate for the change, which for a file nothing compiles can
come down to a single test — the sub-agent still runs, even when what it
has to run is one test. `ui-review` binds when the change can alter what
the game shows a player or asks of them. This file, a test's plumbing and
CI configuration usually give it nothing to read; the build system does
the moment it changes what gets compiled in, since `-DSCORE`, `-DCAPTURE`,
`-DCLOAKING` and the `-DDEBUG` that Debug builds add all decide which
commands and messages the game has at all.

When it is unclear whether a change reaches the player, run the pass. A
`ui-review` with nothing to say costs one pass; code that runs while the
game runs reaches the player whether the change meant it to or not, and a
refactor that preserves behavior is exactly where a lost line hides.

Skipping it is a decision, not an omission. Say that it was skipped and
why — to `code-review` when invoking it, per step 8, and in the commit,
the pull request body and the summary of the work. The last three put it
on the record; the first is the one that reaches a reviewer with a
mandate to argue back, and reaches it before there is a commit to argue
about, which is why step 8 asks for it as well. An agent writing that
sentence about a change to the game's own output has skipped the wrong

claims to implement, the journey a player takes through it, the state

rather than run it. Reaching the same runtime through `node

1	#!/bin/sh
2	# Checks that AGENTS.md stays the single source of truth for project
3	# instructions, and that CLAUDE.md stays a pointer to it.
4	#
5	# Rules drift into CLAUDE.md easily and silently: Claude Code's `#`
6	# shortcut appends there, `/init` rewrites the file wholesale, and
7	# tools that target CLAUDE.md by name edit it directly. None of them
8	# know AGENTS.md exists. Without a check, the result is two sources of
9	# truth that slowly disagree.
10	#
11	# The AGENTS.md checks matter just as much: CLAUDE.md pulls it in with
12	# an `@AGENTS.md` import, and if that file is renamed, emptied, or
13	# deleted the import resolves to nothing -- no error, no warning, just
14	# an agent session with no rules at all.
15	#
16	# Usage: instructions.sh /path/to/repo/root
17	
18	set -u
19	
20	ROOT="${1:-.}"
21	while [ "${ROOT%/}" != "$ROOT" ] && [ "$ROOT" != "/" ]; do
22		ROOT="${ROOT%/}"
23	done
24	CLAUDE="$ROOT/CLAUDE.md"
25	AGENTS="$ROOT/AGENTS.md"
26	
27	# The pointer needs a title, a sentence or two, and the import. Kept
28	# tight on purpose: headroom here is room for a rule to hide by being
29	# folded into an existing line rather than added as a new one, which
30	# the line budget below cannot see. A very short phrase can still fit;
31	# that one is left to review.
32	MAXBYTES=220
33	# CLAUDE.md is meant to be frozen, so this is the exact number of
34	# non-blank lines it has today, not a generous budget: a rule slipped in
35	# as plain prose adds a line and nothing else would. Changing the
36	# pointer's wording means changing this number on purpose. The prose is
37	# wrapped at 72 columns to match the rest of the repo -- rewrapping it
38	# much narrower will need a third line and trip this.
39	MAXLINES=4
40	# Enough that a gutted or stub AGENTS.md fails, well under its real size.
41	MINAGENTS=2000
42	
43	fails=0
44	fail() {
45		printf 'FAIL: %s\n' "$1" >&2
46		fails=$((fails + 1))
47	}
48	
49	if [ ! -f "$AGENTS" ]; then
50		fail "AGENTS.md is missing -- CLAUDE.md's @AGENTS.md import would silently resolve to nothing"
51	fi
52	if [ ! -f "$CLAUDE" ]; then
53		fail "CLAUDE.md is missing -- Claude Code sessions would load no project rules"
54	fi
55	if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
56		exit 1
57	fi
58	
59	agentsbytes=$(wc -c < "$AGENTS" | tr -d ' ')
60	claudebytes=$(wc -c < "$CLAUDE" | tr -d ' ')
61	
62	# AGENTS.md holds the real content.
63	if [ "$agentsbytes" -lt "$MINAGENTS" ]; then
64		fail "AGENTS.md is only $agentsbytes bytes; expected at least $MINAGENTS -- has its content been moved or lost?"
65	fi
66	if ! grep -q '^## Development workflow' "$AGENTS"; then
67		fail "AGENTS.md has no '## Development workflow' section -- the workflow every agent follows should live there"
68	fi
69	
70	# CLAUDE.md points at it and holds nothing else.
71	if ! grep -q '^@AGENTS\.md[[:space:]]*$' "$CLAUDE"; then
72		fail "CLAUDE.md has no '@AGENTS.md' import line -- Claude Code would not load the shared rules"
73	fi
74	# Blank out the one allowed import and see if any other remains. An
75	# import works mid-line too, so matching only at the start of a line
76	# would miss `... see @RULES.md:` -- four lines, small, and a second
77	# source of truth in every session. Only whole tokens are blanked, or
78	# `@AGENTS.md.bak` would be read as the allowed import plus nothing --
79	# and since `.` has to count as part of a token for that, sentence
80	# punctuation after the import is absorbed too.
81	if sed -E 's#@AGENTS\.md([.,;:!?]?)([^A-Za-z0-9._/-]|$)#\1\2#g' "$CLAUDE" \
82			| grep -q '@[A-Za-z0-9._/-]'; then
83		fail "CLAUDE.md imports a file other than AGENTS.md -- rules should reach agents through AGENTS.md alone"
84	fi
85	if [ "$claudebytes" -gt "$MAXBYTES" ]; then
86		fail "CLAUDE.md is $claudebytes bytes, over the $MAXBYTES limit -- rules belong in AGENTS.md, not here"
87	fi
88	
89	claudelines=$(grep -cv '^[[:space:]]*$' "$CLAUDE")
90	if [ "$claudelines" -gt "$MAXLINES" ]; then
91		fail "CLAUDE.md has $claudelines non-blank lines, expected at most $MAXLINES -- if you added a rule, move it to AGENTS.md; if you reworded the pointer, update MAXLINES in this script"
92	fi
93	
94	# Rules arrive as list items or new sections. The pointer needs neither,
95	# so their presence below the title means content landed in the wrong file.
96	if tail -n +2 "$CLAUDE" | grep -qE '^[[:space:]]*(#|[-*+][[:space:]]|[0-9]+\.[[:space:]])'; then
97		fail "CLAUDE.md contains headings or list items below the title -- move that content to AGENTS.md"
98	fi
99	
100	# Claude Code also loads CLAUDE.md files from subdirectories (when working
101	# under them) and from .claude/. Any of those is a second shared source of
102	# truth, so only the root pointer may exist. A personal, unshared
103	# CLAUDE.local.md at the root is deliberately left alone -- .gitignore
104	# keeps it from becoming a shared one.
105	#
106	# Matched case-insensitively: macOS filesystems are case-insensitive by
107	# default, so a lone claude.md there would load like the real thing.
108	# The prune list mirrors .gitignore's build trees rather than any
109	# directory merely starting with "build".
110	extra=$(find "$ROOT" \( -name .git -o -name build -o -name 'build-*' \) -prune -o \
111		-iname 'CLAUDE*.md' \
112		! -ipath "$ROOT/CLAUDE.md" \
113		! -ipath "$ROOT/CLAUDE.local.md" \
114		-print 2>/dev/null)
115	if [ -n "$extra" ]; then
116		fail "these files also carry instructions; fold them into AGENTS.md:"
117		echo "$extra" | sed 's/^/         /' >&2
118	fi
119	
120	if [ "$fails" -ne 0 ]; then
121		printf '\n%d check(s) failed.\n' "$fails" >&2
122		printf 'AGENTS.md is the source of truth for every coding agent; CLAUDE.md only imports it.\n' >&2
123		printf 'Put project rules in AGENTS.md and leave CLAUDE.md as the pointer.\n' >&2
124		exit 1
125	fi
126	
127	printf 'instructions OK (CLAUDE.md %s bytes, AGENTS.md %s bytes)\n' "$claudebytes" "$agentsbytes"
128

**What I want checked hardest.**

1. **The two new checks, adversarially.** I have shipped assertions on this repo that could not fire — an awk regex written `/></` that lexed as `><`, a positive control the defect could erase, an assertion behind an `elif` nothing reached. Lex the awk rather than reading it. The count is done by flattening the file's line breaks and using `gsub` to count, because the phrase wraps mid-sentence in two of the four places; check that the flattening cannot produce a false count, and that `gsub`'s return is the number of matches rather than something else. 4. **Whether the four claimed occurrences are the ones I think.** Three steps plus the section. If the phrase appears anywhere else, or if one of the three steps does not actually contain it and the count is being made up elsewhere, the check passes while the file is wrong.

5. Anything in the new prose that claims more than the evidence carries. The `### Answering a finding` section says a pass has "produced better evidence when disputed" and "has conceded" — that is a claim about this repository's history, and I should not make it if it did not happen.

content.text: Verifier passed it but found the thing that matters most: **the count check degrades to a silent pass if awk fails.** `[ "" -ne 4 ]` errors, `if` reads that as false, and the script prints "instructions OK". A check that quietly stops existing is worse than no check. Fixing that and the four other findings:

input.old_string:
# Counted rather than located: which step is which is the numbering
# check's business, and hard-coding line numbers here would break on
# every edit above them. Counted over the file with its line breaks
# flattened, because the phrase wraps mid-sentence in two of the four
# places it appears -- a check that a rewrap can break is a check that
# will be deleted the first time someone rewraps.
STANDARD='actionable finding, or resolve it explicitly'
standards=$(awk -v want="$STANDARD" '
	{ s = s " " $0 }
	END { gsub(/[ \t]+/, " ", s); print gsub(want, "&", s) }' "$AGENTS")
if [ "$standards" -ne 4 ]; then
	fail "AGENTS.md states the finding standard $standards times, expected 4 -- once each in steps 6, 7 and 8, and once where 'Answering a finding' defines it. If a step reworded it, the steps no longer visibly agree"
fi
input.new_string:
# Counted, not located: hard-coding line numbers would break on every
# edit above them, and nothing here can tell which step a match fell in.
# So this catches the one-place regression -- a step reworded on its own
# -- and not a coordinated edit that reworded a step and added the
# phrase somewhere else to keep the total at four. Issue #65 is the
# check that would know one step from another.
#
# Counted over the file with its line breaks flattened, because the
# phrase wraps mid-sentence in two of the four places it appears: a
# check a rewrap can break is a check that gets deleted the first time
# someone rewraps. The phrase holds no regex metacharacter, so passing
# it to awk as a pattern matches it literally; one added later would
# quietly turn this into something else.
STANDARD='actionable finding, or resolve it explicitly'
standards=$(awk -v want="$STANDARD" '
	{ s = s " " $0 }
	END { gsub(/[ \t]+/, " ", s); print gsub(want, "&", s) }' "$AGENTS")
# A non-number means awk did not run -- unsupported construct, missing
# binary, anything. Left to `[ "$standards" -ne 4 ]` that is not a
# failure but a silent pass: the test errors "Illegal number", `if`
# reads the non-zero status as false, and the script goes on to print
# "instructions OK". A check that stops existing has to say so.
case "$standards" in
'' | *[!0-9]*)
	fail "could not count the finding standard in AGENTS.md -- awk printed '$standards' instead of a number, so this check did not run"
	;;
*)
	if [ "$standards" -ne 4 ]; then
		fail "AGENTS.md states the finding standard $standards times, expected 4 -- steps 6, 7 and 8 each state it and 'Answering a finding' defines it. A step reworded on its own no longer visibly agrees with the others"
	fi
	;;
esac

numerically without checking it is a number. When the command fails, the
comparison errors and the shell reads the non-zero status as *false*, so
the check is skipped and the script goes on to print `instructions OK`.

keeps `CLAUDE.md` a pointer and `AGENTS.md` present. It is the last
place that should fail open.

**#88 is the one to take, and #91 left the fix sitting one line away.**

`make_windows()` now resizes `wstat` and `wmsg` on every repaint but still never touches `wquad` — it's created once and left to `resize_term()`, which shrinks it and never grows it back. That's the whole bug: shrink below 29 columns or 13 rows, come back to 80x24, and the quadrant panel stays stretched with no right border and the prompt gone. A `wresize(wquad, panelh, QUADW)` beside the other two is the likely fix, and `panelh` already exists because #91 needed it.

Why it's the right next slice:

- **Worst player outcome still open.** #90 leaves stale characters in one column; #94 and #95 need a design decision. #88 leaves the display permanently broken *at an ordinary size*, after the player has already returned to one — nothing on screen explains why, and the prompt is gone.
- **It unblocks coverage that's currently impossible.** `draw_quad_line`'s clipping only engages below 29 columns, so the only assertion I could write for it runs at 16x24 and poisons the session. A test at 25x24 that a player could continue from waits on this.

content.text: The naive fix over-corrects: forcing `wquad` to 29 columns makes the title guards see room that isn't on screen. It needs the same clamp `panelh` gives the height:

input.command:
cd /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek
python3 - <<'PY'
p='tui.c'; t=open(p).read()
old = """	panelh = LINES < PANELH ? LINES : PANELH;"""
new = """	panelh = LINES < PANELH ? LINES : PANELH;
	quadw = COLS < QUADW ? COLS : QUADW;"""
assert t.count(old)==1; t=t.replace(old,new,1)
old2 = """	int msgh, statw, msgw, panelh;"""
new2 = """	int msgh, statw, msgw, panelh, quadw;"""
assert t.count(old2)==1; t=t.replace(old2,new2,1)
old3 = """		wresize(wquad, panelh, QUADW);"""
new3 = """		wresize(wquad, panelh, quadw);"""
assert t.count(old3)==1; t=t.replace(old3,new3,1)
old4 = """		   Below the
		   panel's own size the ask fails and the window stays as
		   curses left it, which is the clipped display the player
		   is looking at anyway. */"""
new4 = """		   Asked for at the size
		   the screen can show rather than the size it wants, for
		   the reason panelh exists: a window held at its full width
		   on a narrower screen reports room the player cannot see,
		   and the guards that decide whether a title fits believe
		   it. */"""
assert t.count(old4)==1; t=t.replace(old4,new4,1)
open(p,'w').write(t); print("quadw clamp added")
PY

input.prompt:
Review the player-facing behavior of branch `fix/tui-restore-quadrant-panel` in /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek. Closes #88. Read `AGENTS.md` and anything you check against from the repository, not from a copy in your context. `./build/sst` is current with the working tree; two files changed, `tui.c` and `tests/tui.sh`.

**The bug.** `make_windows()` resized the status and message windows on every repaint but never the quadrant panel — it was created once and left to curses, which shrinks a window that no longer fits and never grows it back. So a terminal squeezed past the panel's own size and returned to a comfortable one came back broken, at a size where nothing on screen explains why. Measured before the fix:

- squeeze to **29 columns or narrower**, return to 80x24 → the quadrant box comes back wider than its 29 columns, its right border merged into the status panel's left one
- squeeze to **13 rows or fewer**, return to 80x24 → the box comes back taller than PANELH, its bottom border gone, and the message window is off the bottom of the screen with the `COMMAND>` prompt on it
- 30 columns and 14 rows both recovered cleanly, which matches what `README.md` already tells a player

**The fix, three parts.** `wresize(wquad, panelh, quadw)` beside the two that were already there; a `quadw` clamp so the panel is asked for the size the screen can show rather than its full width; and `mvwin(wmsg, PANELH, 1)`, because a short squeeze **moves** the message window as well as shrinking it and size alone did not bring it back — the panels returned whole while the conversation stayed gone on a screen with eleven empty rows waiting for it.

**What I want judged, as a games/CLI expert.**

1. **What a player actually gets back.** The panels and the prompt return, but the conversation that scrolled through the message window during the squeeze does not — curses cannot reflow it and the game keeps no transcript. So the player comes back to a working display with an empty conversation. Is that the right recovery, or does it read as a different kind of broken? If you think the game should say something on returning, that is a design call I want from someone who did not write this.

2. **The band below the panel's own size.** At 25 columns or 10 rows the display is clipped and stays clipped — that is #78 and #91's clipping doing its job — but with this change the panel now springs back the moment there is room. Check the transition in both directions and at the exact boundaries (29/30 columns, 13/14 rows), and say if the springing back is jarring or reads as the display simply working again.

3. **Whether anything regressed at the sizes that already worked.** 72x24 and 80x24 are the claim the slice rests on. Also check the damaged-sensors caption and the `>` clip markers, since the `quadw` clamp changes what `panel_room(wquad)` reports at narrow widths and those guards read it.

4. **The repeated-squeeze case.** Squeeze, return, squeeze again, return — several times in one session. I have only tested one round trip per session, and #90 (stale columns outside every window) is nearby.

Known and deliberately not fixed here, both filed: **#94** — below fourteen rows there is still no prompt *while you are down there*; this change only restores it on the way back. **#95** — at fourteen rows the pager has no lines to show. If you hit either, say so rather than reporting a regression.

tmux on **your own socket** (`-f /dev/null -L <your-own-name>`), never the default, never a bare `kill-server`, never `kill-session` on a session you did not create. Report findings only; do not edit files.

cd /home/scottdensmore/Developer/scottdensmore/super-star-trek
gh issue create --title "A resize does not put the pending prompt back, and a corner squeeze leaves a stump of it" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Problem

`sync_size()` restores the line the game is part way through writing
only when the terminal **shrank**. The shrink-time write puts the whole
line into a window that may be one row tall and narrower than the line,
so it wraps, scrolls, and only the tail survives — and nothing repairs
it when the terminal grows back.

After returning to 80x24, with the display geometry otherwise fully
restored:

| squeezed to | what the message area reads |
|---|---|
| 28x13, pause pending | ` ]` |
| 20x8, pause pending | ` CONTINUE]` |
| 20x8, at the first setup question | ` , or frozen game?` |
| 20x8, at end of game | ` core recorded?` |
| 10x8 or smaller | nothing at all |

The 20x8 pause case is worse than cosmetic: typing `srscan` there, the
`s` was eaten by the still-pending pause and `rscan` was read as a
command, so the game answered with the full command list. That is the
swallowed-keystroke shape the banner-pager work was originally about.

At 10x8 and below the player gets a working set of panels above eleven
empty rows and no prompt — #88's own "frozen empty box" symptom, now
reachable only through this path. Pressing Enter re-prompts, but nothing
on screen says so.

## Scope

**Pre-existing**, and verified so: a build of this branch's merge-base
produces the identical ` urnament, or frozen game?` stump from a 30x14
squeeze — a size `main` already recovers from. So it is not a
consequence of #88's geometry restore.

But it is what stands between #88 and its own acceptance criterion,
"shrinking to any size and growing back restores a working display".
After #88 the *geometry* recovers at any size; the pending prompt line
may not. A corner drag is the commonest resize gesture there is.

Related and probably one fix: after a narrow-only squeeze the
conversation stays clipped into the restored wide screen with nothing
marking it — ` Shields       DOWN, 10`, ` Position      3 - 2, 7`,
` Starbase locations-   4 - 5` of four bases. `tui.c`'s own `clip_at()`
comment argues a truncated number is worse than garbage because it reads
as a smaller plausible value; the panels get a `>` for exactly that
reason and the conversation gets nothing.

## Suggested approach

Either reprint the pending pair on a **grow** as well as a shrink — the
joined-row search added for wrapped pairs is what makes that safe now —
or skip the shrink-time write when `curlen + answer > msgw * msgh` and
let the grow-back restore do it.

Whichever way, erasing the rows that can no longer be trusted and
reprinting the live line would resolve the clipped-history half at the
same time, and make the recovery uniform instead of sometimes blank and
sometimes mangled.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] After any squeeze and return, the pending question or pause is on
      screen whole, or the window is clean and the game re-prompts.
- [ ] Covered in `tests/tui.sh`, whose squeeze block now includes a
      corner case (20x8).
- [ ] `README.md`'s paragraph on what comes back stays true.

Found by `ui-review` on the branch for #88. Follow the workflow in
[AGENTS.md](../blob/main/AGENTS.md).
EOF
)"

Closes #88. Read `tui.c`, `tests/tui.sh`, `README.md` and anything you fact-check against from the repository, not from any copy in your context.

**The defect.** `make_windows()` resized the status and message windows on every repaint and never the quadrant panel — created once and left to curses, which shrinks a window that no longer fits and never grows it back. Squeeze past the panel's own size and return, and the display stayed broken at a size where nothing explains why: the quadrant box back too wide with its right border merged into the status panel, or too tall with the message window and prompt hidden under it.

**The fix, three parts in `make_windows()`:**
1. `wresize(wquad, panelh, quadw)` beside the two already there.
2. A `quadw = COLS < QUADW ? COLS : QUADW` clamp, so the panel is asked for what the screen can show. Without it the window reports room the player cannot see and the title/caption guards from #78 believe it — the mutant trips those pre-existing guards, not the new block.
3. `mvwin(wmsg, PANELH, 1)` **after** the resizes. `resize_term()` shifts a window whose origin sits at or past the screen bottom, so a short squeeze moves the message window as well as shrinking it.

**Passes.** `ui-review` twice, `verifier` twice, and both failed the branch once:

- `ui-review` round 2 blocked on `README.md`, which documented the defect this branch removes and told the player to quit and restart a game they need not lose. Rewritten to its wording.
- `verifier` round 1 found part 3 in the **wrong order**: `mvwin` ran before the resizes, and `mvwin` refuses a move that would not fit at the window's current size, so a squeeze *wider* than the terminal returned to (82x13 → 80x24) left the move refused and the conversation permanently off-screen — the display looking right while swallowing input. It found the cause by probing ncurses rather than inferring it. My comment had the rationale backwards. Reordered; `"82 13"` added to the test loop, and I proved it isolates the ordering.
- `verifier` round 2 passed after an exhaustive probe: 115,200 prior→destination pairs, 0 bad in the new order against 2,840 in the old.

**Since that pass** I made two changes it has not seen, both from its own report: dropped `"10 8"` from the loop (it fired identically to `"20 8"` on every break — a case that cannot fail alone), and rewrote the block's comment to say which two sizes are coverage and which two are diagnosis. Suite re-run green.

**What I want scrutinised:**

- **Whether `mvwin`'s ignored return value is really fine.** The verifier established it returns `ERR` exactly when `LINES <= 13` or `COLS < 2`, and that those are the harmless "nowhere legal to go yet" cases because `make_windows()` runs again on the next repaint. I accepted that. It is the kind of thing I would rather have two readers on.
- **The `quadw`/`panelh` pair.** Both clamp a constant against the screen; `statw` and `msgw` next to them clamp differently (`> 1 ? : 1`). Say if the two idioms sitting together will mislead.
- **Whether keeping `25 24` and `80 13` is right** when `20 8` catches everything they do. I kept them for diagnosis and said so in the comment; the verifier called that defensible but wanted it not to read as coverage.
- Anything in the comments or the README that claims more than the evidence carries. Three of my claims in this change came back wrong — the mvwin ordering rationale, and two README claims `ui-review` falsified.

**Filed, not fixed:** #100 (the pending prompt comes back a stump after a deep squeeze — pre-existing), #101 (the `tui` test's timeout comment says ~11s; it is ~68s), #94, #95.

I reran the mutant with the quadrant `wresize` removed: 8 failures, and the width ones now read "the wrong width". Suite 11/11, `tui OK`, `shellcheck` clean.

Two things to check rather than confirm:

2. **Whether the README's new qualifier is in the right place.** I put it on the paragraph about resizing generally, not on the one about deep squeezes. If it reads as hedging the ordinary case — where the question and answer genuinely do survive, and that is a feature #46 and #79 were built for — then it belongs somewhere else or nowhere.

**The fix turned out to be three parts, and I got two of them wrong first.**

- `wresize(wquad, ...)` was the part I expected. But forcing the full width made the panel report room the screen doesn't have, so the `#78` title guards started drawing past the edge — hence a `quadw` clamp.
- `mvwin(wmsg, ...)` I found only because the panels came back perfect above eleven blank rows: a short squeeze *moves* the message window, it doesn't just shrink it.
- And I called `mvwin` **before** the resizes, which `mvwin` refuses when the window is still too wide for the destination. So 82x13 → 80x24 left the conversation off-screen permanently — a display that looked right and silently swallowed everything typed into it. The verifier found that by probing ncurses rather than reasoning, then confirmed the reorder across 115,200 size pairs: zero bad, against 2,840 in my order.

**One process error worth naming.** `code-review` caught that no `ui-review` had seen the reordered code — the verifier's finding arrived *after* the last screen-reading pass, and the line it changed is exactly the one that decides what a player sees. That's step 6's rerun rule, and I'd reported the passes without flagging the gap. Round 3 has now run on the real state.

### 1. The corrected mechanism — right, and I measured the two ways it could have been wrong

I probed ncurses with three windows on one screen: A 13x29 at column 0, B 13x29 at column 51 (right edge flush against column 79 at 80 columns), C 13x20 at column 10.

| screen | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| 80 → 60 | 29 (untouched) | 29 (untouched, now hanging off the right edge) | 20 |
| 60 → 80 | 29 | 29 | 20 |
| 80 → 25 | **25** | **25** | 20 (untouched, hanging off) |
| 25 → 80 | **80** | **80** | 20 |

- **It is spanning, not touching an edge.** B sat flush against the right edge at 80 columns and the 80→60 squeeze ignored it entirely. Position never mattered in either direction: B, at column 51 and wholly off-screen at 25 columns, grew to 80 exactly as A did.
- **It is spanning, not "no longer fits at its position" either.** C hung nine columns off the right edge at 25 columns and was left alone, because its *width* still fitted the screen.

So the grow-back trigger the comment names — a window as wide as the screen follows the screen — is exactly the rule. The one compression is the "down" half: what gets cut down is a window *wider than the screen*, which is what makes it span in the first place. Your next clause, "a panel squeezed past its own size stops being 29 columns and starts tracking the terminal", already states that condition precisely, so the sentence as a whole predicts the symptom the test asserts. No change needed.

Worth knowing but not worth writing down: this is also why `wquad` was the only casualty. `statw` is `max(COLS-QUADW,1)` and `msgw` is `max(COLS-2,1)`, so neither is ever wider than the screen and curses never resizes them behind the code's back; `wmsg`'s only mistreatment is the `begy` shift, which is the separate below-the-bottom rule your second comment covers on its own. The two comments already split the two mechanisms correctly.

### 2. The README qualifier is in the right place

Keep it where it is. It qualifies the one sentence that can fail, and a reader who stops after the second paragraph would otherwise carry away an absolute promise the fifth paragraph then contradicts — which was the whole finding. It does not hedge the ordinary case, because in the ordinary case the condition is met and the sentence reads as the promise it was: the paragraph immediately below ("Dragged smaller than the 72x24 the panels ask for…") is what tells the reader when room runs out, so "still room for them" resolves within a few lines rather than dangling. Moving it down to the deep-squeeze paragraph would restore the contradiction; dropping it would too.

The only thing I would even raise is rhythm, and it is optional: the clause currently interrupts the promise before it is made ("and so long as there is still room for them, both the question … survive"). Trailing it — "and both the question you were asked and the answer you were halfway through typing survive, so long as there is still room for them" — keeps #46 and #79's feature in the main clause and the condition as a caveat. Take it or leave it; both are accurate.

### On the tightened width assertion

I confirmed it catches the narrow direction and not only the wide one. In an outside-the-repo copy I capped the quadrant panel at 20 columns on resize; the block reported `restore: after 25x24 the quadrant panel came back the wrong width` and the same at 20x8 — the two cases where the screen had actually been narrow, which is where a too-narrow restore can arise. (The two height-only squeezes stayed green there because the cells between a 20-wide panel and the status panel still held stale border glyphs from the initial 29-wide draw. That is an artifact of the mutant only: in the real code `quadw` is `min(COLS, QUADW)`, so no such gap can exist.) The renamed message is the right call — it matches what the check can prove.

**No.** `AGENTS.md` says nothing about it. The only two mentions of Codex are unrelated: it's listed as one of the agents the file governs, and `codex exec` is named as how a non-Claude agent gets its own reviewer.

The plugin work from earlier is fully reverted — but that was the **Claude Code plugin** (`/codex:review`). What reviewed #99 is a different thing that's still live: the `chatgpt-codex-connector` GitHub app, configured repo-wide, which comments on PRs when they're opened. Removing the plugin didn't touch it.

So there's a real gap, and it's structural rather than cosmetic:

- **The workflow ends at step 12.** Every review pass is pre-commit; the bot arrives *after* the commit and the PR exist. Nothing says who addresses its findings, whether threads must be resolved, or whether a fix needs a fresh `verifier`/`code-review` round. On #99 I invented all of that — second commit, replies, resolved threads, both passes rerun — with no rule behind it.
- **Its findings don't gate anything.** Step 12 says merge when "every configured check passes." The bot posts *comments*, not checks, so a PR with unaddressed P2s is still `CLEAN MERGEABLE`. #102 is in exactly that state right now: green, mergeable, and the bot hasn't posted yet.
- **It has earned a place.** On #99 it found two real P2s, one of which was a silent-pass hole in a guard that `code-review`, the `verifier` and I had each built a fake-`awk` matrix against. A fourth reader with no memory of the first three caught it in one pass.

Two things I'd want your call on before writing anything:

1. **Do its findings bind?** Treating them like `code-review` findings — fix or explicitly resolve, per the standard #97 just landed — is the consistent answer. But it's a bot on someone else's infrastructure, and making it blocking means a PR can be held by a service you don't control.
2. **Does the PR wait for it?** Right now I could merge #102 before it comments. A rule saying "wait for the bot, or say you didn't" is cheap; a rule saying "wait indefinitely" isn't.

# Codex Code Review Triggers and Reactions

## Triggers

Codex code reviews are initiated through explicit mentions. The documentation states: **"In a pull request comment, mention `@codex review`."** Reviews do not run automatically on every push unless you enable the automatic review feature.

For automatic reviews, the docs note: **"If you want Codex to review every pull request automatically, turn on **Automatic reviews** in Codex settings. Codex will post a review whenever someone opens a new PR for review, without needing an `@codex review` comment."**

So there are two modes:

The documentation mentions one reaction explicitly:

The eyes emoji (👀) indicates that Codex has acknowledged your request and is processing the review. The document does not explain what a thumbs up reaction signifies in this context.

Every pull request here is reviewed by Codex, through a GitHub app the
repository has turned on. Nobody asks it to; opening the pull request
starts it, and so does every push afterwards. It is the fourth reader
in this workflow and the only one that arrives after the commit exists.

It says what it is doing with reactions on the pull request itself.
👀 means it is reviewing. Then either it posts review comments, or it
reacts 👍 and posts nothing — 👍 is not approval of the change, it is
"this pass found nothing to say".

So the loop is: push, wait, read what it left, answer every comment,
push the answer, wait again. **Its comments bind exactly as
`code-review`'s do** — fix, or resolve explicitly, on the standard
"Answering a finding" sets. Reply on the thread rather than only in the
commit: the thread is where the disagreement reaches the reviewer, and
it is where the next reader looks. Then resolve the thread, which is
what says the answer is given rather than merely typed. Repeat until a
push comes back 👍, and only then merge.

Do not merge a pull request whose comments are answered but whose
answering push has not been reviewed. Every push is a new review
because every push is a new change, and the round that matters is the
one that saw the state being merged — the same rule step 8 applies to
`ui-review`, arriving from the other end of the workflow.

Two things this cannot promise. It is a service on someone else's
infrastructure: if it never reacts, that is a fact to report and a
judgment for the person merging, not a reason to invent an approval it

The rule is written and waiting on the final verdict. **The single most important thing this round produced is a correction to what you asked for**, and it's worth stating plainly before I commit anything:

**The merge condition you described can't be satisfied as stated.** GitHub allows one reaction per user per issue. Once the bot has 👍'd a PR it *cannot add a second one*. So the ordinary sequence — 👍 on open, you push a fix, the re-review finds nothing — leaves the original 👍 sitting there with its original timestamp, and no new 👍 ever arrives. "Keep going until you see the thumbs up" works the first time and silently degenerates after that: you'd be waiting for something the platform cannot produce, or reading a stale 👍 as approval of a push it never saw.

What the file says instead: after a push you're waiting for **comments or their absence**, absence isn't something GitHub reports, so give it the few minutes a review takes, look for new comments, and record what you saw. `gh api repos/:owner/:repo/issues/<n>/reactions` is the only place the reaction's timestamp is visible at all — the web UI doesn't show it.

Two other corrections to the premise: the "every push" trigger is a **setting**, not inherent behaviour, and the enumerated trigger list I'd cited turns out to document Codex *Security Review* — a different product. And the bot **does** read `AGENTS.md`; both its comments on #99 cited this file by line range, at rules rather than at the diff.

Also filed **#103**: Codex documents a `## Code Review Rules` section as the supported way to steer it, and we don't have one — so it's inferring what matters from the whole file.

Restored, with the actual numbers: #104 opened `05:46:08Z` and had comments at `05:49:47Z`; the push run answered in 2m24s with 👀 up five seconds in. Both under four minutes.

If the bot *doesn't* withdraw an existing 👍, no newer one can arrive at all and step 12's condition becomes permanently unsatisfiable — the failure case, not the solved one. 3. **"the rule in step 12 rests on that, and it was reasoned before it was watched"** contradicted the sentence after it. Step 12's rule is being introduced *by* this rewrite, after the observation. Cut.
4. **"Neither" had grown a third antecedent** — one paragraph had quietly bundled two claims. Split into four, "None of those".
5. **A fourth measured claim sat outside the block that enumerates what's measured** — that a no-findings pass files no review object. Now listed there.
6. The 👀 withdrawal time is **inferred** from when the comments posted, not observed (GitHub keeps no history of a removed reaction); the gap is three quarters of an hour, not two thirds; and a dangling appositive read as though the 👍 *was* the withdrawn 👀.

# the heading, and a pointer above it. Neither implies the other, and
# each fails silently on its own -- a heading nothing references is a
# section no reader is sent to, and a pointer with no heading under it
# sends them nowhere. So both are checked, for every section a step
# defers to by name.
#
# The pointer is matched in quotes because the heading itself is
# unquoted, so this finds the reference and not the thing referred to.
# Before the heading, specifically: a mention below it is a
# back-reference and cannot send anyone anywhere, since the reader is
# already there. Counting quoted mentions was enough while "Answering a
# finding" had one pointer and one heading, and stopped being enough the
# moment a later section quoted the name too -- that alone would satisfy
# a count while step 6's pointer was deleted, which is the state this
# exists to catch.

# pointer is a quoted phrase in wrapped prose, and a rewrap that split
# it across two lines would fail here while the pointer sat there
# intact. What it cannot see is which step the pointer is in, or a
# layout that put the section above the steps -- the second would fail
# it wrongly, and is why the messages say what was checked rather than
# what it means.
check_section() {
	name="$1"
	why="$2"
	if ! grep -q "^### $name" "$AGENTS"; then
		fail "AGENTS.md has no '### $name' section -- $why"
		return
	fi

		{ all = all " " $0 }
		END {
			gsub(/[ \t]+/, " ", all)
			h = index(all, "### " s)
			q = index(all, "\"" s "\"")
			print (q > 0 && h > 0 && q < h) ? "yes" : "no"
		}' "$AGENTS"); then
		fail "could not look for the pointer to \"$name\" in AGENTS.md -- awk exited non-zero, so this check did not run"
		return

#
# The third argument is a floor under the section's body, in the same
# spirit as MINAGENTS above and for the same reason: the heading and the
# pointer are two lines, and a section gutted to a stub satisfies both
# while saying nothing. It is a floor, not a budget -- set well under
# the real size, so ordinary editing never touches it and only a
# deletion does. It cannot tell whether what is there is still the right
# content; nothing here can, and that is what review is for.
#
# Bodies run from the heading to the next `### ` or the end of file.
# Counted in whatever units awk gives -- characters under a UTF-8
# locale, bytes under C -- because a floor this far below the real size
# does not care which.
check_section() {
	name="$1"
	why="$2"
	minbody="$3"
	if ! grep -q "^### $name" "$AGENTS"; then
		fail "AGENTS.md has no '### $name' section -- $why"
		return
	fi
	if ! body=$(awk -v h="### " -v n="$name" '
		index($0, h n) == 1 { inb = 1; next }
		inb && index($0, h) == 1 { inb = 0 }
		inb { b += length($0) + 1 }
		END { print b + 0 }' "$AGENTS"); then
		fail "could not measure the \"$name\" section of AGENTS.md -- awk exited non-zero, so this check did not run"
		return
	fi
	case "$body" in
	'' | *[!0-9]*)
		fail "could not measure the \"$name\" section of AGENTS.md -- awk printed '$body' instead of a number, so this check did not run"
		return
		;;
	esac
	if [ "$body" -lt "$minbody" ]; then
		fail "AGENTS.md's \"$name\" section is down to $body characters, under the $minbody floor -- $why. If you shortened it on purpose, lower the floor in this script on purpose"
	fi

docs: rewrite the Codex section from what was measured

The section this branch added reasoned about the bot's reactions instead
of watching them, and reasoned wrong. It said a 👍 could not be repeated
-- one reaction per user per issue -- so a pull request that drew one on
opening would keep it, timestamp and all, however many pushes followed.
On that footing the reaction was useless after a push and the section
told a reader to watch the comments instead.

Pushing 50540ea tested it, with nothing else touched on #104: 👀 five
seconds later, 👍 at 06:36:41Z, and no review object and no comments
behind either. So the bot swaps its reaction rather than accumulating,
a 👍 can postdate the push it answers, and a pass that finds nothing
files no review at all -- which makes an unchanged comment count
evidence of nothing, and the reaction the whole of the answer. Step 12
can therefore ask for a 👍 newer than the last push, which is what the
first version of this branch wanted and could not have.

Reading that comparison takes two calls, and the second one is where
this went wrong three times over. It first said GitHub serves no push
timestamp: false, and `repos/:owner/:repo/events` returns this branch's
to the second. Then it filtered that feed to `PushEvent`, which a
branch's first push does not file -- only a `CreateEvent`, with the ref
in a different shape -- so the recipe returned nothing for every branch
in this repository never pushed to twice, which is the ordinary case
and 27 of the 29 in the feed. Then it printed the call without
`--paginate` beside the three hundred events only `--paginate`
returns; the default page is thirty, about a day here. All three are
fixed, and the fallback -- note the time yourself -- now attaches to
the lag as well as the limits.

Two smaller things came out of the same reading. A review the bot posts
carries `**Reviewed commit:**` and a sha, which answers "did it read my
state" outright wherever there are comments, leaving the timestamp
comparison to the silent pass alone. And the withdrawal of a 👀 is
dated from the comments that replaced it, not watched: GitHub keeps no
history of a reaction taken back, so the section says which of its
claims are measured, which are reasoned, and which are neither.

tests/instructions.sh grew a guard for the section. The two per-section
checks were factored into check_section() and are now called for "The
Codex review" as well, with a third: a floor under the section body,
because a heading and a pointer are two lines and a section gutted to a
stub satisfies both. Before this, deleting all 110 lines of the section
left the suite green. Proven by mutation outside the repository -- body
gutted, heading renamed, each pointer unquoted, each of the four
statements of the standard reworded -- and by fifteen awk fault
injections, all caught and attributed to the right check.

ui-review did not run and is not owed: one instruction file and one
shell test that reads markdown, nothing compiled, no feature flag, no
string the game prints. cppcheck, clang-tidy and scan-build are absent
from this machine, so no static analyser ran; nothing here compiles, so
the cost is nil, but it is a gap rather than a pass.

Also filed: 105, for the prefix match that lets a heading renamed to
"### The Codex review process" satisfy every one of these checks while
the pointers name a heading that no longer exists. It predates this
refactor -- the two inline checks it was factored out of matched the
same way -- and is named in a comment beside the checks it limits.

input.content:
`chatgpt-codex-connector[bot]` reviews every pull request in this
repository, and the workflow never mentioned it. So its findings had no
standing, its threads had no rule, and step 12 could merge a pull
request with unanswered comments — the bot posts *comments*, not
checks, so nothing about the merge state knew they were there.

It has earned the place. On #99 it found a silent-pass hole in a test
guard that `code-review`, the `verifier` and I had each built a fake-awk
matrix against and each missed.

Its comments now bind as `code-review`'s do: fix, or resolve explicitly,
on the standard "Answering a finding" sets. Reply on the thread, resolve
it, and where the answer was a fix, push it and let the review run on
what you pushed.

## The rule this nearly shipped the opposite of

An earlier version of this branch argued that "wait for the thumbs up"
**cannot be followed**: GitHub allows each reaction only once per user
per issue, so a pull request that draws 👍 on opening could never draw a
second, and waiting for a fresh one was waiting for something the
platform cannot produce.

That was reasoned, not observed, and it was wrong twice over. Pushing
`50540ea` with nothing else touched drew 👀 five seconds later and a
**new** 👍 at 06:36:41Z, from a pass that filed no review object and no
comments at all. So the bot swaps its reaction rather than accumulating
it, and a 👍 can postdate the push it answers.

Step 12 therefore asks for exactly what the earlier draft called
impossible: a 👍 whose `created_at` is later than your last push.

## The experiment this branch called in advance

That still left the narrower question the first run could not reach —
#104 was carrying *nothing* when `50540ea` landed, so nobody had seen
what happens to a 👍 already standing. The section said so and named the
push that would settle it. That push was `6ed975b`, at 23:35:58Z, with
#104 carrying the 06:36:41Z 👍:

| time | reactions on #104 |
|---|---|
| 23:36:05Z | `+1` @ 06:36:41Z — the old one, still there at +7s |
| 23:36:17Z | `+1` gone, `eyes` @ 23:36:08Z |
| 23:39:48Z | `eyes` gone, `+1` @ 23:39:48Z |

No review object and no comments at any point. So a standing 👍 **is**
withdrawn — but not instantly, and for something like the first twenty
seconds the stale one is still on screen looking exactly like an
answer. That is the argument for reading the timestamp and never the
icon.

## What the passes took out of my prose

Across the rounds, `verifier` and `code-review` between them removed:
the claim that GitHub serves no push timestamp at all (two API calls
disprove it); a recipe filtered to `PushEvent`, which a branch's *first*
push never files — 27 of 29 branches here have only a `CreateEvent`, so
it returned nothing for the ordinary case; a command printed without
`--paginate` beside the 300 events only `--paginate` returns; a
universal drawn from one observation; a measurement attributed to a
commit that did not contain it; "gone by ten seconds" where the polls
only bracket it at seven to nineteen; three counts that the next push
would silently falsify; and a sha anchor that stops resolving the moment
step 12 squash-merges and deletes the branch.

Two of those I introduced *while fixing* an earlier finding, and one of
those two came from a `code-review` suggestion I applied without
checking it. Both are noted here because the file's whole subject is
telling what was measured from what was assumed.

The section now sorts every claim into documented, measured (naming the
pull request and the timestamps), or still unwatched — and the unwatched
entries each name the review that would settle them.

## Test changes

`tests/instructions.sh` grew a guard for the section this branch adds.
Before it, deleting all 110 lines of "The Codex review" left the suite
green. The two per-section checks were factored into `check_section()`,
called now for that section too, with a third check: a floor under the
section body, since a heading and a pointer are two lines and a section
gutted to a stub satisfies both.

Proven by mutation outside the repository — body gutted, body trimmed
just under the floor, heading renamed, each pointer unquoted, each of
the four statements of the standard reworded — and by fifteen awk fault
injections, all caught and attributed to the right check.

The floor was raised 4000 → 6500 after the `verifier` found it had
drifted: the section was 7954 characters when the floor was written and
13141 now, so 4000 had fallen from half the body to under a third.

## Disclosures

- `ui-review` did not run and is not owed: one instruction file and one
  shell test that reads markdown, nothing compiled, no feature flag, no
  string the game prints.
- `cppcheck`, `clang-tidy` and `scan-build` are absent from this
  machine, so no static analyser ran. No C changed, so the cost is nil,
  but it is a gap rather than a pass.
- The Codex thread on this pull request is answered and resolved. Its
  finding — that "then push" was unconditional, giving an agent an
  impossible step when a finding is resolved rather than fixed — was
  right and is fixed.
- Filed: #105, for a prefix match that lets a heading renamed to
  "### The Codex review process" satisfy every one of these checks while
  the pointers name a heading that no longer exists. It predates this
  refactor and is named in a comment beside the checks it limits.
- The withdrawn-reaction observations above are unrecoverable by
  construction — GitHub keeps no history of a reaction taken back — so
  they rest on the polling recorded here. #99's and #102's 👍s are
  frozen and still checkable; #104's have to be taken on trust.

gh issue create --title "Nothing runs shellcheck on tests/*.sh, in CI or in ctest" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
The repository has four shell scripts under `tests/` that are part of the test
suite, and nothing lints them. `shellcheck` appears in neither `CMakeLists.txt`
nor `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```sh
grep -rn 'shellcheck' CMakeLists.txt .github/
# (no matches)
```

## Why it matters

`tests/instructions.sh`, `tests/golden.sh`, `tests/tui.sh` and
`tests/tournament.sh` are the suite's only check on several things the compiled
tests cannot see, and they are written to be portable POSIX `sh`. The failure
mode for a shell test is not a crash — it is a check that silently stops
checking. This branch and #99 between them have already produced three of those
by hand:

- `[ "" -ne 4 ]` errors and `if` reads the non-zero status as false, so the
  script printed `instructions OK` with the defect present (filed as #98 for
  the three remaining instances)
- an awk regex written `/></` which lexes as `><`
- an assertion chained behind an `elif` that no input could reach

`shellcheck` would not have caught all three, but it is the cheap layer that is
missing entirely, and it catches the class where a construct does not mean what
it looks like.

## Current state

`shellcheck -s sh tests/instructions.sh` is clean today — I ran it by hand
while working on `docs/codex-pr-review`, which is the point: it only ever runs
when someone remembers.

## How to see it

```sh
grep -rn 'shellcheck' CMakeLists.txt .github/workflows/ci.yml   # nothing
shellcheck -s sh tests/*.sh                                     # runs, and is not wired to anything
```

## Fix sketch

Either a ctest entry alongside the existing `instructions` test, skipping when
`shellcheck` is absent the way `tui` skips without `tmux` — and failing rather
than skipping when `$CI` is set, which is the pattern `tests/tui.sh` already
uses — or a step in the CI workflow. The ctest route keeps it runnable locally
and matches how the rest of the suite is wired.

Note that the scripts target POSIX `sh`, so `-s sh` matters: the default
dialect detection will accept bashisms the scripts must not have.

## Provenance

Found by the `verifier` sub-agent while verifying `docs/codex-pr-review`
(#104). Pre-existing and repository-wide, so filed rather than fixed in that
slice, per AGENTS.md step 9.
EOF
)"

The merge gate had a real hole, and it's the kind that only bites in production.

**`gh api .../reactions` returns *everyone's* reactions, all marked `+1`.** Step 12 says merge once a 👍 postdates your last push — so a maintainer thumbs-upping their own agent's PR after the final push produces exactly the shape the gate looks for, and the merge proceeds **with no Codex pass having run at all**. The section spends whole paragraphs on why `pushed_at` can't be used and on the `CreateEvent`/`PushEvent` split, then left this one to inference from a login named 37 lines earlier. Now it carries the filter explicitly.

Two more:

- **My character count was off by one, and the reviewer diagnosed exactly why** — splitting on `\n` keeps a phantom empty record after the file's final newline. awk saw 228 records, I counted 229. Recomputed properly, both agree at 235 records: **14090 bytes / 13903 characters**.
- **The `Answering a finding` floor was 71% of its section** — a budget, not a floor, and against the policy the comment right above it argues for. That section is four paragraphs, so deleting one would have tripped it, and the failure message would have invited lowering the number, which is precisely how a floor decays. Now 850, the same half the other one sits at, with the reasoning beside the call.

Both floors mutation-tested and firing. gh issue create --title "instructions.sh floors go slack silently when a section grows" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
`check_section()` in `tests/instructions.sh` takes a floor under each guarded
section's body, so a section gutted to a stub fails even though its heading and
its forward pointer survive. The floor is aimed at about half the section.

The check is one-sided, and the side it does not cover is the one that happens
without anyone noticing.

## What is wrong

A floor only speaks when its section **shrinks**. Nothing speaks when the
section **grows** away from the floor, which is what actually happens over
time — and each time it does, the floor guards proportionally less.

Measured on `docs/codex-pr-review` (#104), with the function's own awk:

| commit | `The Codex review` body | floor | floor as % of body |
|---|---|---|---|
| `6ed975b` (added the check) | 7954 | 4000 | 50% |
| that branch's next change | ~14100 | 4000 | 28% |

Two thirds of the section could have been deleted silently, one change after
the floor was written. It was raised to 6500 by hand, but only because a
reviewer happened to measure it — nothing in the suite would ever have said so.

`tests/instructions.sh` says this about itself, and then does nothing about it:

> Nothing prompts anyone to revisit this. The check only speaks when a
> section shrinks, and the condition worth noticing -- a floor left far
> under a section that grew -- is silent by construction.

## Why it matters

The floor is the only thing standing between a guarded section and a silent
gutting, and its strength decays with every edit that adds to the section. A
check whose value quietly erodes reads, from outside, exactly like a check that
is working.

## Fix sketch

A companion upper bound: fail when `body` exceeds some multiple of `minbody` —
say 3× — with a message saying the floor has fallen behind its section and
naming the number to raise it to. That turns "the floor has gone slack" from a
hope into a message, which is what the existing comment asks for and cannot
deliver as prose.

The multiple wants to be loose enough that ordinary growth does not nag. 3×
against a floor aimed at half the body gives room for a section to grow by half
again before it complains.

Note the units wrinkle: the awk counts bytes under mawk and characters
elsewhere, so any bound wants the same slack the floor has.

- `tests/instructions.sh` — `check_section()`, and the comment block above it
  that already describes the gap.

## Provenance

Raised by the `code-review` sub-agent while reviewing #104, as a design change
belonging to a different slice rather than a defect in that one. The drift it
describes was found by the `verifier` sub-agent on the same branch, three times
in one session.

### should-fix — `tests/instructions.sh:293`: the self-invocation has no recursion guard, so a broken `--body` dispatch hangs and leaks processes instead of failing

`check_section` re-enters the script with `sh "$0" "$ROOT" --body "$name"`, relying entirely on the child taking the `--body` branch at line 47 and leaving at the `exit 0` on line 66. If it does not — I tested it by deleting that `exit 0`, which is the same class of edit the other three mutations were — the child runs the full checks, reaches `check_section`, spawns another child, and so on without bound.

The failure mode is worse than a hang. Observed: a chain of `sh tests/instructions.sh . --body Answering a finding` processes each parented to the previous, still growing at ~800 processes after two minutes, and orphaned to PID 1 when the driver was killed. `ctest` sets `TIMEOUT 30` on this test, so CI would report a timeout while the chain kept forking after the test was reaped. Recovery is also awkward: killing a mid-chain process returns from the parent's command substitution, and the parent then goes on to the *second* `check_section` and starts a fresh chain — I had to restore the script before the kills would stick.

This matters precisely because the mutation that triggers it is the one this check exists to catch. Every other way of breaking `--body` produces a clear failure; the one that stops the dispatch firing produces a hang.

Suggested fix, two lines and it lands in the message the check already has. In `check_section`:

```sh
if ! flag=$(INSTRUCTIONS_BODY_CHILD=1 sh "$0" "$ROOT" --body "$name" 2>&1); then
```

and immediately after the `--body` block's `fi` at line 67:

```sh
# The child above is only ever invoked with --body, so getting here with
# the marker set means the dispatch stopped firing. Refuse rather than run
# the checks again: check_section would re-invoke, and so on -- which hangs
# instead of failing, and leaves the chain running after ctest's timeout
# kills the top of it.
if [ "${INSTRUCTIONS_BODY_CHILD:-}" = 1 ]; then
	printf '%s: --body did not dispatch; refusing to recurse\n' "$0" >&2
	exit 2
fi
```

On your other two questions, no defect: `sh "$0"` is the right re-entry — it survives a lost exec bit, and it resolved correctly under every invocation form I tried; and the two new exit statuses are coherent (2 for usage/missing file, 1 for a content failure, matching the script's own exit 1), with `check_section` treating any non-zero as "the recipe does not work".

### nit — `tests/instructions.sh:47-67`: nothing exercises the new guards

`check_section` drives only the happy path, so the empty-name guard, the missing-file guard and the missing-heading guard are new executable code that no run touches; a future edit that reordered them past the `awk` would go unnoticed, which is the exact hazard the empty-name guard was added for. One more assertion in `check_section` covers them for the price of the one already there — e.g. assert that `sh "$0" "$ROOT" --body ''` exits 2 — and would also cover the recursion guard above.

### nit — `tests/instructions.sh:61`: `--body` accepts a name that only matches as a regex, and answers `0`

`grep -q "^### $3"` treats the name as a BRE while the awk matches it literally, so a name with a metacharacter can pass the guard and measure nothing:

```
$ sh tests/instructions.sh . --body 'The C.dex review'
0
```

Exit 0, and a reader re-aiming a floor gets a number rather than an error. The comment at lines 178-182 already notes this divergence for `check_section`, where the names are literals under the author's control; here the input is a human's typing, which is what the guard beside it is for. Cheapest close: after the awk, refuse a measurement of 0 with the "no such section" message.

The reviewer found a **fork bomb**, and it was mine.

My self-check re-invokes the script, trusting the child to take the `--body` branch and leave. Delete that `exit` — the same class of edit as the three mutations I'd used to "prove" the check — and every child runs the full checks, re-invokes, and forks again. The reviewer measured **~800 processes still growing after two minutes**, orphaned to init, outliving the `ctest` timeout that reaps the top of the chain. Worse, killing a mid-chain process just returns control to its parent, which starts a *fresh* chain on the next section.

The bitter part: that's the one break the check exists to catch. Every other way of breaking `--body` fails loudly; the one that stops the dispatch firing hung instead.

Fixed with a marker on the child and a refusal at the point the branch falls through. Reproduced the exact mutation: it now exits 1 in under a second with `--body did not dispatch; refusing to recurse`, no orphans.

Two nits also fixed:
- **The guards were unreached code** — `check_section` only ever drove the success path. Three assertions now exercise them, including the recursion guard.
- **`grep -q "^### $3"` was a BRE while the measurement is literal**, so `The C.dex review` passed the guard and returned `0` as though it were an answer. The guard now rejects on the measurement itself, so there's no second matcher to disagree with the first.

`shellcheck` clean; `sh`/`dash`/`bash`/`busybox` all pass; `ctest -R instructions` green.

I said last round was the last. It wasn't, and I'd rather say so than pretend — a fork bomb in a test script is worth the round. This state adds a guard against unbounded recursion, which is exactly the kind of thing I shouldn't be the only reader of, so I'll take one look at it and then commit whatever comes back short of a real defect.

docs: record what the Codex reviewer actually did

The section this branch added called one case unwatched and named the
push that would settle it: a pull request already carrying a 👍 that
then takes a push. Pushing 6ed975b was that push. #104 was carrying the
06:36:41Z 👍 at the time; seven seconds after the push it was still
there, by nineteen it was gone with 👀 in its place, and at 23:39:48Z
that gave way to a 👍 of its own, with no review object and no comments
filed. So a standing 👍 is withdrawn to start the next cycle, which is
what step 12's rule needs, and it is not withdrawn instantly, which is
why the rule reads a timestamp rather than looking for an icon.

Nothing else here is new work. It is the corrections the review passes
took out of the section, and they are worth listing because the section
is about telling what was measured from what was assumed.

The recipe for the push time was wrong three ways in succession: it
said GitHub serves no push timestamp, which two API calls disprove;
then filtered the events feed to PushEvent, which a branch's first push
never files, so it returned nothing for every branch never pushed to
twice; then printed the call without --paginate beside the three
hundred events only --paginate returns. Reading the reaction was wrong
twice: the endpoint returns every user's, and a human thumbs-up carries
the same +1 as the bot's, so filtering on neither field would have let
a maintainer's own reaction clear step 12's gate with no review having
run -- and filtering on the user alone would have handed back the bot's
in-progress 👀 as though it were an answer. Both are now one --jq away.

Smaller ones, in a section that has no business making them: a
universal drawn from one observation; a measurement attributed to a
commit that did not contain it; "gone by ten seconds" where the polls
only bracket it at seven to nineteen; a platform rule about reactions
that is not one; counts and shas that the next push or the next squash
merge would quietly falsify. Two were introduced while fixing an
earlier finding, and one of those came from a review suggestion taken
without checking it.

tests/instructions.sh needed the same treatment. Its floor comment
quoted the section's size, which every edit to the section changed, so
the figure was stale before the commit carrying it could land -- twice,
each time caught by a reviewer reading a number that reproduced against
nothing. No current size is written down now. The measurement is a
flag, tests/instructions.sh . --body '<section>', running the same awk
the floor is compared against, and check_section re-invokes it and
fails if the two disagree, so the recipe cannot drift from the check in
silence.

That self-invocation then had to be made safe. A break that stopped the
--body dispatch firing -- deleting its exit, mistyping the flag -- gave
every child the full checks, another re-invocation, and an unbounded
fork chain that outlived the test timeout reaping the top of it, which
is the one break the check exists to catch. It now refuses rather than
recurses. The --body guards are driven by three assertions, since
check_section otherwise only ever reached the success path.

Floors re-aimed to about half their sections. 4000 was half of "The
Codex review" when it was written and under a third one change later;
1200 was over 70% of "Answering a finding", which is a budget, and a
budget gets lowered reflexively until it means nothing.

ui-review did not run and is not owed: one instruction file and one
shell test that reads markdown, nothing compiled, no feature flag, no
string the game prints. cppcheck, clang-tidy and scan-build are absent
from this machine, so no static analyser ran; no C changed, so the cost
is nil, but it is a gap rather than a pass.

Resolved rather than fixed: probe_body '' compares only an exit status,
and dash exits 2 when sh "$0" cannot open the script, the same 2 the
empty-name guard returns. Under sh -s < tests/instructions.sh that one
assertion could pass for the wrong reason while the other two fire. It
is a blind spot in one assertion rather than a hole in the check, the
run fails loudly either way, and the invocation form has no usable $0
and cannot reach CI.

Also filed: #106, for shellcheck not being wired into ctest or CI, and
#107, for these floors being one-sided -- they speak when a section
shrinks and are silent when it grows away from them, so their strength
decays with every edit while looking from outside exactly like a check
that works.

## The rule's first live use — it works

| | |
|---|---|
| push (from the events feed) | `02:16:14Z` |
| 👍 withdrawn, 👀 up | `02:16:22Z` — 8s |
| fresh 👍 | `02:19:04Z` — 2m50s |
| step 12's condition | **met** — 👍 postdates the push |
| unresolved threads | 0 · merge state **CLEAN** |

Two things validated themselves on first use. My noted push time matched the feed **exactly**, because the branch now says to note it *after* `git push` returns — the six-second error that correction came from. And the standing 👍 was withdrawn again, a second independent instance of the behaviour the whole section rests on.

I deliberately did **not** edit that third observation into the file. It would invalidate the approval and restart the cycle to add a data point that changes no conclusion.

## What landed

Two commits. `6ed975b` rewrote `### The Codex review` from measurement after the first experiment disproved my reasoning; `989aad0` records the second experiment and the corrections the passes extracted.

**The defects worth naming**, because they'd have burned someone:

- **The merge gate could be satisfied without a review running.** The reactions endpoint returns everyone's reactions and a human's 👍 carries the same `+1` as the bot's — so a maintainer thumbs-upping their own agent's PR cleared step 12. Filtering by user alone then returned the bot's *in-progress* 👀 as an answer.
- **The push-time recipe returned nothing for the common case** — a branch's first push files no `PushEvent`. 27 of 29 branches here.
- **A fork bomb in the test script.** My own recipe self-check re-invoked the script with no recursion guard, and the one mutation it existed to catch was the one that hung instead of failing.

## Filed

**#105** prefix-matched headings · **#106** `shellcheck` unwired from ctest and CI · **#107** the floors are one-sided and decay silently as a section grows.

## On the record

- `ui-review` did not run and is not owed — one instruction file and one shell test; nothing compiled, no feature flag, no string the game prints. Stated to `code-review`, in the commit, and in the PR body.
- `cppcheck`, `clang-tidy`, `scan-build` are absent from this machine. No C changed, so the cost is nil — but no static analyser ran.
- **Resolved rather than fixed:** `probe_body ''` compares only an exit status, and dash exits 2 when `sh "$0"` can't open the script — the same 2 the guard returns. A blind spot in one assertion, inside a run that can't be green, on an invocation form `add_test` never produces. In the commit and PR body.

content.text:
`check_section()` — it asserts three things about a section that a numbered step hands work to:

1. **The heading exists** — `grep -q "^### $name"`
2. **Something above it points at the name in quotes** — so a step can't defer to a section nobody is sent to. It requires the mention to come *before* the heading, since one after it is a back-reference and sends nobody anywhere.
3. **The body clears a floor** — because a heading and a pointer are two lines, and a section gutted to a stub satisfies both while saying nothing.

It's called twice:

```
check_section 'Answering a finding'  … 850
check_section 'The Codex review'     … 6500
```

Your commit tripped **#1** on the second call. The message is the whole diagnosis:

```
FAIL: AGENTS.md has no '### The Codex review' section --
      it is the only place the reviewer that steps 11 and 12 defer to is defined
```

The reasoning behind it: `AGENTS.md` is a file where deleting a section is silent. Nothing compiles it, nothing renders it, and a step that points into thin air reads perfectly fine to whoever wrote it. Before this check, deleting the whole section left the suite green.

**Two honest caveats now that it's fired on you:**

The floor number is a judgement I made, not a fact — 6500 against a 14,426-character section. If you'd trimmed the section to 4,000 characters rather than removing it, the check would have failed too, and it would have been the *check* that was wrong, not your edit. That's why the failure message tells you to lower the floor on purpose, and it's what **#107** is about.

And it can't tell "deleted by mistake" from "deleted deliberately, and the pointer needs updating too." It only knows a step points somewhere that isn't there. Here it's the second — so the fix is to the pointer and the check, not to restore anything.
